entries.title: Kimi K3 on 8 GB of RAM: how a 2.78T model runs with no GPU
entries.caption:
Kimi K3, a 2.78-trillion-parameter AI model, ran in 8 GB of RAM with no GPU. The catch is your disk, not your RAM.
Free setup guide: https://withhammad.com/resources/kimi-k3-on-8gb-ram

How kimi-k3-in-c, an Apache-2.0 C engine by Fareed Khan, does it:
- About 93% of Moonshot AI's 1.56 TB checkpoint is mixture-of-experts weights.
- Those experts stay on a fast NVMe SSD, and each token reads only 16 of 896 experts per layer.
- Output is byte-identical from 8 GB to 224 GB of RAM. More memory changes the speed, not the answer.

What it really costs:
- About 1.7 TB of free disk before you download a single byte.
- Hours of downloading (about 3.5 hours at 1 Gbps).
- About 30 seconds per token, measured on a 124-core server with its RAM capped at 8 GB.
- On an 8 GB Jetson board with a hard drive, one word ("Paris") took nearly 16 minutes.

So treat it as a proof of concept, not an everyday app: text only, no server, no quality benchmark.

For UAE businesses that handle client data, the interesting part is privacy. A model you run locally keeps prompts on your own machine; a hosted API sends them to another company's servers. The memory wall did not disappear. It moved to your disk.

Kimi K3 is open weights under Moonshot's own Kimi K3 License, a custom license rather than an OSI open-source one. The engine is Apache-2.0.

The video says "comment BYTES"; that is for Instagram. Here the guide is one click, no comment needed: https://withhammad.com/resources/kimi-k3-on-8gb-ram

Would you trade speed for keeping your data on your own hardware?

entries.title: AI search traffic converts better? How to track your own AI traffic in GA4
entries.caption:
One Semrush study found AI search visitors 4.4x as valuable as organic, by conversion rate. Here is how to track AI traffic in GA4 and test it on your own numbers.
Free setup guide: https://withhammad.com/resources/ai-traffic-ga4

Why it can happen: people research inside ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini before they click, so they arrive further down the funnel than someone scanning search results.

The stat, honestly: Semrush (Jul 2025) found the average AI search visitor 4.4x as valuable as an organic search visitor, based on conversion rate. It is one vendor study. Other studies range from about 1.3x to over 20x.

So measure your own AI referral traffic:

1. Check your AI visibility. Ask ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini the questions your customers ask. Are you mentioned, and described correctly?
2. Open GA4 > Reports > Acquisition > Traffic acquisition and find the AI Assistant channel (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and more).
3. Add "AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini...)" to your "Where did you hear about us?" form.
4. Split those customers out and compare conversion rate and order value against search and social.

Two caveats: Google AI Overviews and AI Mode stay in Organic Search, not the AI Assistant channel. And many AI clicks arrive with no referrer and land in Direct, so the channel undercounts.

That is why GEO/AEO work needs measurement before budget moves.

Full guide with the custom channel group setup: https://withhammad.com/resources/ai-traffic-ga4

Have you seen AI Assistant traffic in your GA4 yet?

entries.title: NVIDIA SkillSpector: scan Claude Code skills before you install them
entries.caption:
Scan Claude Code skills before you install them: NVIDIA SkillSpector is free and gives each skill a 0-100 risk score.
Free setup guide: https://withhammad.com/resources/skillspector-scan-skills

Why Claude Code security starts with skills: a Jan 2026 study of 31,132 marketplace agent skills (Liu et al.) found 26.1% had at least one vulnerability, and 5.2% showed high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent. Confirmed malicious skills are rarer (157 of 98,380 in a follow-up, all removed), but one bad skill could still leak your API keys.

How to use NVIDIA SkillSpector:
1. Install it with uv from NVIDIA's GitHub: uv tool install git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git (on Python 3.14, add --python 3.12)
2. Scan a skill folder, GitHub link or zip. To check all your skills: skillspector scan ~/.claude/skills --recursive --no-llm
3. Read the score: 0-20 low, 21-50 caution, over 50 do not install.
4. Keep --no-llm on for private or client skills, so the code stays on your machine.

It checks 17 risk categories, including prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse and MCP tool poisoning. On its own test skills (Oct 2026), the safe one scored 0/100, the malicious one 100/100.

The honest caveat: a low score means no red flags were found, not that a skill is proven safe. In our --no-llm test it missed the natural-language attack samples; the optional LLM review covers those but sends files to your model provider. It is a scanner, not a sandbox, and it is not on PyPI, so install it only from NVIDIA's repo. Treat it as one layer of AI agent security.

The video's SCAN DM is Instagram-only; here the guide is one click: https://withhammad.com/resources/skillspector-scan-skills
